Strategy Posts Record $20.9 Billion Q3 Book Profit, but Bitcoin per Share Falls 3.7%
sum: Strategy (MSTR.US), which holds the largest corporate Bitcoin position in the world, reported fiscal 2026 third-quarter results, booking a $20.91 billion (about NT$680 billion) digital asset fair-value gain as Bitcoin prices rebounded, pushing both operating income and net income to record highs. But behind the stellar headline numbers lie structural contradictions: a shrinking core software business and a decline in Bitcoin per share. The market's reaction was muted.

According to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) dated October 29, Strategy's third-quarter operating income reached $20.91 billion, more than quadruple the $3.89 billion (about NT$130 billion) posted a year earlier. Net income was $19.53 billion (about NT$630 billion), with diluted earnings per share of $44.75, far above the $8.42 reported a year earlier. Net income attributable to common shareholders was $19.12 billion (about NT$620 billion), after deducting $419.6 million (about NT$14 billion) in preferred stock dividends.

The massive profit did not come from operating cash flow but from a book adjustment under accounting rules. Under fair-value accounting, Strategy revalues its Bitcoin holdings at market prices each quarter and books the change directly on its income statement. Bitcoin rose in the third quarter, sharply inflating the carrying value of its 848,517 coins. Excluding the digital asset fair-value gain, software revenue was just $125.4 million (about NT$4.1 billion), down 3% from a year earlier and below the $127.2 million analysts had estimated. For context, the $20.91 billion Bitcoin revaluation gain is roughly 167 times software revenue—a gap that is key to understanding the report.

Outgoing Chief Financial Officer Andrew Kang said in a statement: "Strategy's $21 billion in operating income in the third quarter is the highest level in the company's history." He also emphasized that amid a challenging Bitcoin market environment, the company has increased its Bitcoin holdings by 26% so far this year.
As of October 25, Strategy held 848,517 Bitcoin, up 26% from the start of the year, at an average acquisition cost of $75,446 per coin.

Strategy Bitcoin buying pause: $204.9M share buyback

Here is what the filing shows: the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin bought no Bitcoin at all in the week of October 19 to 25, 2026. Instead, $204.9 million went into the repurchase of 2.07 million of its own STRC preferred shares, paid out of cash on hand. Our own reading follows further down: Strategy is tidying up its dividend burden rather than growing the stack.

The short answer to the question every holder is asking: nothing was sold. The stack still stands at 848,517 Bitcoin. Only the buying has stopped, and so far only for one week. The company reports these figures every Monday in a mandatory filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the 8-K. The filing dated October 26, 2026 is the source for every number in this article.
What Strategy reported for the week of October 19 to 25, 2026

Three items sit at the heart of the filing. First, no Bitcoin transaction, neither a purchase nor a sale. Second, no share sales through the running at-the-market programme, the mechanism the company uses to issue new stock continuously on the exchange. Third, $204.9 million for the repurchase of 2.07 million STRC preferred shares.

That ends a run of weeks in which the company added to the stack every time. How long that run actually was depends on who is counting: one reading puts it at five consecutive weeks, another at three. Both refer to the same mandatory filing and differ only because some of those weeks brought token amounts. We give the range rather than smooth it over.

A pause in buying is nothing new at Strategy. The company has reported weeks without a purchase several times before, and after one longer pause it even sold. What is new is the scale of what happened instead.

sum: Bitcoin is trading below $81,993, the average entry price for net long positions, increasing pressure on investors betting on higher prices.

On Oct. 24, blockchain media outlet U.Today reported that Coinbase Markets said on X, formerly Twitter, that the average entry price for the area with the highest concentration of Bitcoin net long positions was $81,993.

A published chart showed 64 percent of net long notional was entered at levels above the spot price. That suggests a substantial amount of long positions may be sitting on losses. If prices fall further, forced liquidations of leveraged long positions could increase selling pressure.

Liquidations were concentrated in long positions. Bitcoin traded at $80,595, down 1.50 percent over 24 hours. Over the same period, total liquidations across the crypto market were $481.25 million, of which long liquidations accounted for $346.15 million. Bitcoin liquidations were $95.06 million, with $85.9 million in long liquidations far exceeding $9.16 million in short liquidations.

The key question is whether investors increase positions in expectation of a rebound or reduce exposure to avoid further losses. Coinbase pointed to whether traders add positions on hopes of a rebound or cut exposure to reduce additional losses as the key issue.

Demand to hedge against declines also stood out in the options market. In a separate post, Coinbase said Bitcoin option prices reflect a clear downside bias across the entire volatility curve. Bitcoin 25-delta skew was 11.3 percent for 1-day expiry, 10.5 percent for 1-week expiry and 10.8 percent for 1-month expiry, while the 1-year figure was 3.9 percent. That means implied volatility for put options is higher than for calls with the same terms, and the bias is stronger in short-dated contracts than in longer-dated ones.

With spot weakness intersecting with a cautious mood in derivatives markets, attention is on whether Bitcoin can recover $81,993, a key long entry price. Reclaiming that level could ease some pressure on underwater positions, but a further decline could raise the possibility of increased selling pressure from liquidations.

Sygnum and Debifi Launch MultiSYG: Bank-Backed, Multisig Bitcoin Loans with Client Control
sum: Sygnum and Debifi have rolled out MultiSYG, a Bitcoin-collateralised lending product that brings multisignature, shared-control custody into a bank-backed loan offering.

Launched on October 23, MultiSYG gives each borrower a dedicated Bitcoin wallet whose signing keys are split between the client, Sygnum Bank and independent institutional key holders. Funds and transactions are governed by Bitcoin Script rules, so no single compromised key can move collateral—and movements can be verified on-chain.

- Custody and control: Collateral stays client-owned, kept off Sygnum’s balance sheet and described as bankruptcy-remote. Authority to spend is distributed across multiple signers rather than concentrated at the bank.

- Parties and safeguards: The signing model involves three types of participants (client, Sygnum, independent key holders). However, the launch did not disclose the specific signing threshold, interest rates or loan-to-value (LTV) limits—those details are in product documentation and client agreements.
- On-chain transparency: Holdings and transfers can be audited on-chain, providing visibility into where collateral sits.

- Lending mechanics: MultiSYG provides fiat liquidity without forcing an immediate sale of crypto. Pledged assets are not rehypothecated; interest accrues daily on the utilised balance; locked collateral has transfer restrictions but excess collateral remains accessible.

- Risk and margin: Wallet security reduces custodial risk but does not eliminate lending risk. Sygnum emphasises continuous risk monitoring and margin management: if Bitcoin’s price drops, borrowers may face margin calls or need to reduce debt regardless of how securely coins are stored. Using the loan preserves exposure to future Bitcoin price movements while simultaneously creating a debt and interest obligation.

sum: Bitcoin’s [BTC] latest recovery appears increasingly dependent on leveraged Futures buying rather than Spot demand alone. Futures Open Interest (OI) grew 8.04% to $27.12 billion within 24 hours. Despite that, BTC retraced to below $82,000 at press time.

This rise suggests traders are opening new positions to capture further gains, adding momentum to the recovery. However, as seen in prior rallies in August and September, these large increases in OI were followed by sharp declines in price and multiple sell alerts.

Increases in leverage therefore can provide significant impetus to an increase in price. However, they can also make a trader very susceptible to being forced into liquidation at a loss. Since Futures OI is trending back up after a fall-off in October.
Sustained buying could support further gains. Still, if investor sentiment begins to deteriorate, then there could be a cascade of forced liquidations and a larger drop in price.

The dominance of Bitcoin derivatives has weakened significantly as traders continue to use leverage to bet on altcoins. Historically, Bitcoin has held over 90% of all OI. In contrast, currently it accounts for less than half, 42.6%, against altcoins’ 57.4%.
This reversal accelerated from 2022, when the percentage of Bitcoin’s leveraged contracts plummeted and the use of altcoin contracts became much more widespread among large exchange users.

As such, this indicates that there is an opportunity for investment in altcoins beyond Bitcoin. However, this may also mean that the potential for greater losses due to a rapid decline in price for the same altcoins may be dispersed throughout a wider range of assets.

Coinbase pushes Bitcoin's post-quantum migration
sum: Coinbase published a position paper on the future of Bitcoin signatures on October 13, 2026. Its central claim is that the move to schemes a quantum computer cannot break has to begin before such a machine exists. Bitcoin is untouched by it at around $81,600 (CoinGecko, October 16). The paper names neither a deadline nor an activation mechanism, and that is precisely its message: the debate is starting, the implementation is not.
Coinbase sets out a position paper on post-quantum migration

The document carries more weight than the usual industry comment, because Coinbase custodies around five percent of all existing Bitcoin according to consistent reports, mostly for banks, asset managers and hedge funds. A firm holding that much of other people's money does not carry migration risk in theory.

The company's reasoning is set down verbatim in the paper: "Bitcoin consensus changes and ecosystem migrations can take years, so it is important that we begin this work now." Elsewhere it states that preparation should start "well ahead of any CRQC". CRQC stands for cryptographically relevant quantum computer, meaning a machine actually strong enough to break today's signatures. No such machine exists so far; the most capable known devices work with fewer than 1,000 qubits.

For the timing, the paper cites an estimate by Google researchers under which a CRQC could emerge around 2029. That number is someone else's forecast, not a commitment by Coinbase, and the expert debate rates it differently.
Technically the paper rests on one idea that is the real point of the proposal: the container of a Bitcoin output and the signature scheme used to spend it later should be separated from each other.

Under the name Pay-to-Merkle-Root, or P2MR, BIP-360 describes an output type that is not tied to one particular signature scheme. A Merkle root is the condensed root of a hash tree, under which several possible spending conditions can be hidden without all of them being disclosed. Its advantage during migration is that a new, quantum-safe scheme can be added later without changing the output format again.

When prompted, Google Gemini AI predicts that by January 1, 2027, Bitcoin could be trading for $175,000. It gives a hypothetical catalyst: the United States announces a landmark, multi-trillion-dollar financial strategy that accelerates Bitcoin accumulation, while several major sovereign wealth funds and pension systems simultaneously introduce substantial Bitcoin allocations.

The announcement triggers one of Bitcoin’s most explosive rallies, fueled by renewed institutional buying and a notable short squeeze. While extreme, this scenario isn’t entirely unrealistic: the US has established a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, and access to Bitcoin through spot ETFs has grown significantly.

Over the next 11 weeks, several key developments could unfold. The US may dramatically expand its Bitcoin Reserve with a bipartisan agreement for a multi-year acquisition program, exceeding market expectations. Major international investment and sovereign funds could treat Bitcoin as a strategic reserve asset.

Regulatory clarity could let pension funds expand access to Bitcoin ETFs, boosting institutional demand. If Bitcoin breaks above $100,000, a short squeeze could force bearish traders to close positions and ignite the rally.

For this scenario to materialize, governments and institutions must commit to substantial new buying. With Bitcoin’s supply capped at 21 million coins, higher demand could drive significant price moves, especially with thin selling liquidity. However, announced reserve holdings don’t guarantee actual purchases, and ETF access alone doesn’t ensure inflows. This scenario assumes real, sustained buying beyond just positive headlines.

items.t: Ether's liquidity shrank vs bitcoin in Q3. XRP bids piled up
sum: - Ether’s price rose more than bitcoin in the third quarter.
- But the token’s liquidity thinned out relative to bitcoin, according to Coingecko.

Ethereum's native token ether had a better third quarter than bitcoin . Still, it got harder to trade, as liquidity, or how easily a token can be bought and sold without moving its price, thinned out.

Ether's price surged 70% in the quarter, outpacing bitcoin's 42% gain. Yet between July 6 and Sept. 30, its median daily market depth was just 35% to 45% of bitcoin's, according to a report by CoinGecko. In the same period last year, it was at least 60%. CoinGecko called it "a stark drop from last year's figures."

Market depth is the standard way to measure liquidity. It's the total dollar value of buy and sell orders sitting on exchanges within a set distance of the current price. The deeper the market, the more money it takes to move the price. In a thin market, a large order quickly eats through available orders and pushes the price further.

Ether had $13 million to $14 million in depth within 0.15% of its market price. In simple terms, that's roughly how much money was sitting in orders close enough to the price that clearing it would move ether by just 0.15%. Depth this close to the price matters most for everyday trades, and for large orders that traders want filled without moving the market.
The data undercuts a popular idea in markets that rising prices pull in more traders, and more traders mean deeper order books. That didn't happen with ether.

Billionaire Tim Draper Predicts Bitcoin Will Hit $250,000 Within 2 Years. Here's What Needs to Happen.
sum: Silicon Valley venture capitalist Tim Draper now expects Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) to hit a price of $250,000 within the next 2 years. If that sounds familiar, that's because it is. For nearly five years, Draper has been banging the table for Bitcoin to hit that mark.
So what's different this time around? Let's take a closer look at what could catalyze a tripling in the value of Bitcoin by 2028.

Over the past few years, Draper has proposed several potential catalysts that could send Bitcoin skyrocketing. His overarching idea has always been that growing rates of adoption, spurred by easier everyday use of crypto, will send the price of Bitcoin much higher.

For example, Draper has suggested that Bitcoin might one day become much more popular for daily commerce. Think of retailers preferring to be paid in Bitcoin rather than dollars. Or rich crypto investors using Bitcoin to buy homes, cars, and big-ticket luxury goods. Bitcoin, after all, is a digital currency originally conceived by Satoshi Nakamoto for peer-to-peer transactions.

Draper has also suggested that demographic changes might spur much higher rates of Bitcoin adoption. At one time, he suggested that closing the gender gap in crypto might lead to more women investors using Bitcoin. He has also suggested that younger generations, growing up as crypto natives, might be more willing to buy, hold, and use digital assets such as Bitcoin.

Overall, Draper has painted a rosy, optimistic view of the future powered by blockchain technology, innovations (such as smart contracts), and digital assets. Over time, traditional financial intermediaries will be swept away, leading to lower costs and greater efficiency. At some point, Bitcoin will become so easy to use that it will be impossible to ignore.

Unfortunately, all of these catalysts have failed to materialize as planned. Bitcoin has never come close to hitting $250,000. The closest it came was in October 2025, when it hit a price roughly one-half of that ($126,000).

For bitcoin traders holding bullish futures bets, $57,000 is the key level, not because it counts as key support from where the market turned higher in early June, but because that’s the level where their bullish bets could be at risk.
Understanding why starts with knowing how futures function and the concept of liquidation, the forced closure of leveraged bets by exchanges due to margin shortage.

Futures allow a trader to control a large position by depositing only a small amount as collateral upfront. The rest is effectively fronted by the exchange, in the form of leverage. If the bet works as expected, all’s well, and gains get amplified because the position is so much larger than the collateral behind it. But if the market does the opposite of the bet, losses get amplified the same way, and once those losses eat through the trader’s margin, the exchange steps in and closes the position automatically.
For the current cohort of longs, $57,000 is the level where positions turn underwater enough that exchanges may have to liquidate, unless traders step in with more collateral.

It eked out a nearly 2% gain in March, following five consecutive down months. Ether gained 8% in the same period, also its second up month in a row and best month since August.

Perpetual futures — the dominant source of leveraged crypto trading activity — was the "sole driver" of the rally, however, according to CryptoQuant. The firm's apparent demand metric, which tracks the 30-day change in outright purchases of bitcoin, stayed negative throughout April while futures demand rose.
The two trends combined are often a warning sign, according to Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant. They suggest the upward price action is fueled by speculation rather than fundamentals.

"This divergence – rising futures demand alongside contracting spot demand – suggests price appreciation is driven by leverage rather than fresh coin accumulation," Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, said in a report Thursday. "Historically, such configurations lack the structural foundation required to sustain price gains and typically resolve via correction once futures positioning unwinds."
The data also underscores the shifting environment for crypto exchanges and importance of crypto derivatives – which include perpetual futures and, increasingly, prediction markets.

Perpetual futures, better known as "perps," continue to be the dominant venue for trading activity, liquidity and price discovery. At the same time, spot trading, which early crypto exchanges were built around, is becoming a less reliable engine for steady revenue because it depends on sustained accumulation cycles, which aren't always present.

U.S. regulators' first joint guidance on applying securities laws to different types of crypto tokens failed to provide enough impetus to lift bitcoin , the largest, above $75,000.

However, underneath, its structure looks much less comfortable.

Data shows spot activity fading while derivatives keep doing more of the work. Almost every day this month saw derivatives trading at roughly nine times the spot volume, and that's not the profile of a market pushed forward by spot demand. What we're seeing now is a market propped up almost exclusively by leverage.

While the distinction between Bitcoin spiking due to spot demand and spiking due to increased leverage might sound too technical, the consequences of this setup are very simple and affect everyone and everything.

Spot trading means that someone buys BTC that's been put up for sale and takes possession of the coins. It's a very binary way of assessing demand: if a lot of people want to pay to own Bitcoin and keep it, its price will inevitably increase. If nobody wants it, the sellers have to lower their prices until they find willing buyers, decreasing its global value.

But derivatives are different. They're sophisticated financial instruments that enable traders to run complex trading strategies with futures, options, basis trades, and short-term hedges, often with leverage layered on top.

These strategies keep activity high and the price moving, but they create a market that looks deeper than it really is. When too much of the action sits in derivatives, price becomes more volatile, dependent on positioning, and more vulnerable to abrupt air pockets once liquidations start.

sum: Bitcoin briefly sank below $61,000 on Thursday evening as investor confidence continued to falter in the asset once hailed as "digital gold" and a unique store of value.
At one point, the token slid to $60,062.00, as the crypto sell-off intensified in overnight trading. Bitcoin was last down about 15% at 7:37 p.m. ET, trading at $62,448.00.

Digital assets, including bitcoin, have fallen deeper into the red as investors re-assess the practical utility of a token that has been championed not only as a hedge against inflation and macroeconomic uncertainties but also as an alternative to fiat currencies and traditional safe-havens such as gold.
That hasn't panned out lately, since bitcoin peaked just north of $126,000 in early October.

The cryptocurrency broke below the key level of $70,000 earlier in the session Thursday and then the selling increased, bringing the asset closer in line with its pre-election level. The cryptocurrency is down almost 30% this week alone.

"This steady selling in our view signals that traditional investors are losing interest, and overall pessimism about crypto is growing," Deutsche Bank analyst Marion Laboure said Wednesday in a note to clients.

Growing investor caution comes as many of the sensationalized claims about bitcoin have failed to materialize. The token has largely traded in the same direction as other risk-on assets, such as stocks, particularly during recent geopolitical and macroeconomic flare ups in Venezuela, the Middle East and Europe, and its adoption as a form of payment for goods and services has been minimal.

sum: The bitcoin price briefly climbed above $92,500 today after U.S. inflation data came in line with expectations as markets assessed the Federal Reserve’s policy outlook and rising political tensions surrounding the central bank.
The consumer price index rose 2.7% year over year in December, unchanged from November and matching economists’ estimates, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
On a month-over-month basis, headline inflation increased 0.3%, also in line with forecasts.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 2.6% from a year earlier, compared with expectations for 2.7% and a prior reading of 2.6%. Core inflation increased 0.2% month over month.
December’s CPI report cleared late-2025 “data fog,” bolstering the soft-landing narrative and raising the odds of further Fed cuts, according to Matt Mena, Crypto Research Strategist at 21shares.

“The cooling core data, paired with the jobs data, seem to be inline with the fed’s dual mandate and increase chances of further cuts this year even amidst the political noise surrounding the DOJ’s investigation into Chair Powell,” Mena wrote to Bitcoin Magazine. “Bitcoin is increasingly behaving as a sophisticated macro hedge; in a world of weaponized energy and heightened geopolitical tensions, Bitcoin is being repriced as an international reserve that remains indifferent to sovereign border disputes.”

Bitcoin, which had been trading just below $92,000 around the time of the report, spiked to around $92,800 in the minutes following market open before retreating to roughly $92,300. The cryptocurrency was up about 1%–1.7% over the past 24 hours at the time of writing.

sum: These holders use existing collateral to fund positions without buying delta outright first, making them net sellers when they sell calls.

Market makers purchasing these covered calls must hedge their exposure by selling spot Bitcoin, which forces prices down despite strong demand from traditional exchange-traded fund investors. The problem stems from how these transactions affect market dynamics differently than fresh capital inflows.

When traditional ETF investors buy IBIT and sell calls against it, they add net positive delta to the market because they purchase the ETF at 100% delta, then sell calls at 20-50% delta. Most ETF flows represent true inflows coming into Bitcoin for the first time, creating genuine new demand.

This covered call strategy explains the relentless selling from Bitcoin whales documented since 2021, even before ETF launches. The monetization of existing collateral through options creates adverse effects because it adds long gamma across dealer desks, forcing market makers into dynamic hedging that recreates mean reversion around various strikes.

BlackRock's IBIT ETF shows major divergence in upside skew compared to native Bitcoin options on platforms like Deribit. IBIT displays positive call skew premium in the 120-150% range over longer durations, while Bitcoin skew remains downward sloping through 150%, indicating traditional participants buy upside volatility while crypto-native participants sell it.

IBIT options reached $41 billion in open interest as of Dec. 12, representing over 50% of total assets under management and doubling in under six months. However, Deribit's open interest also grew to around $46 billion, meaning IBIT has not materially closed the gap despite explosive growth.

The analysis concluded that Bitcoin price remains steered by the options market and will stay choppy as long as whales continue to extract short-term profits from their stash by selling covered calls instead of holding or selling spot.

These price swings may seem large but they are normal in relation to bitcoin's history.

Bitcoin's price movement is often referred to in "cycles." Generally, the bitcoin cycle refers to a four-year pattern of price movement that revolves around a key event known as the halving, a change to mining rewards that is written in bitcoin's code. While there are signs that the typical timing and patterns of the cycles could be changing, the range of price movements appears to be consistent.
In the current cycle, bitcoin has already weathered a 32.7% pullback from March to August 2024 and a 31.7% decline between January and April 2025, according to CoinDesk Data.
"Looking at previous cycles, volatility of this magnitude appears consistent with long-term trends," Jacob Joseph, senior research analyst at CoinDesk Data, told CNBC.

In this cycle alone, there have already been five examples where similar consolidations ended with significant moves exceeding 65% gains within 100 days. Averaging those historical fractals to today’s setup would imply a potential bitcoin price target between $170,000 and $180,000 by 2026 if the next expansion phase mirrors prior behavior.

However, bitcoin price volatility compression does not guarantee immediate upside. Previous examples have shown that these low-volatility periods can extend for several months before a breakout occurs. Bitcoin could continue to trade sideways through late Q1 2026, oscillating within the current range before direction is decided.

Several macro factors could serve as a catalyst for renewed bitcoin price volatility. The Federal Reserve is expected to announce another rate cut, which markets currently price at near-certainty. Gold’s recent reversal after setting new highs also hints at potential capital rotation. If even a small fraction of that capital migrates toward Bitcoin amid falling rates and renewed risk appetite, the effect could amplify any breakout once volatility expands.
Volatility naturally declines as Bitcoin matures from a multi-billion to a multi-trillion-dollar asset, but the cyclical nature of expansion and contraction remains.

Bitcoin Price Falls To $110,000 As Institutions Move Millions
sum: Bitcoin price slipped from 24-hour highs near $116,000 to around $110,000 overnight, as large on-chain movements from both the U.S. government and BlackRock fueled speculation about potential institutional repositioning.

According to on-chain analytics, the U.S. government transferred 667.6 BTC, worth roughly $74.8 million, to a new wallet early this morning. The move immediately sparked concerns that the coins — likely seized from prior law enforcement actions — could be en route to an exchange for liquidation.

The transfer likely stems from the U.S. government’s August 2025 conviction of Sergei Potapenko and Igor Turogin in the Hashflare mining fraud case, according to Alex Thorn, Head of Firmwide Research at Galaxy Digital.

Rather than a sale, the move appears to mark the formal forfeiture of the Bitcoin to U.S. government control — either for custody under the Attorney General or for use in the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve.
Around the same time, BlackRock deposited $371 million in ETH and $78 million in BTC to Coinbase, a transaction that some traders speculated could be a signal of upcoming portfolio rebalancing.

The move down to $110,000 follows what has been one of Bitcoin’s most volatile stretches in years. The broader market is still digesting last week’s dramatic plunge, when over $19 billion in positions were liquidated within hours — the largest single liquidation event in crypto history.
More than 1.6 million traders were forced out of positions as cascading margin calls swept across exchanges, triggering an 80% drawdown in various crypto and many altcoins.
